newsitem.title: JAPAN: Three Japan brokers no comment on possible probe.
newsitem.headline: Three Japan brokers no comment on possible probe.

text.p: Spokesmen for three big Japanese brokerages on Friday declined comment on a newspaper report that prosecutors were poised to investigate them in connection with a high-profile racketeer payoff scandal that has already ensnared giant Nomura Securities Co Ltd.

Mass circulation Mainichi Shimbun said on Friday that prosecutors had firmed up their intention to probe the other three of Japan's "Big Four" brokerages for suspected violations of securities and commercial laws in deals with Ryuichi Koike, the "sokaiya" racketeer at the heart of the scandal.
The three are Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd, Daiwa Securities Co Ltd and Nikko Securities Co Ltd.

The Mainichi said prosecutors would make a final decision soon on whether to join the government securities watchdog, the Securities and Exchange Surveillance Commission (SESC), in its ongoing investigation of the three brokerages.
A Yamaichi spokesman said he had not heard of any illegal deals and that the brokerage was continuing its internal checks, but declined comment on a possible move by prosecutors.

A Daiwa spokesman also said he was not aware of any illegal transactions and that Daiwa was continuing to cooperate with the SESC investigation, while a Nikko spokesman declined comment on the Mainichi article.
An SESC executive said early this month that the three firms were cooperating with its investigation but had told the industry watchdog they had not found any illegal deeds so far.
Koike's lawyer has said Koike told prosecutors the three brokerages did illegal discretionary stock deals for him.

Discretionary deals by brokerages are banned by Japan's Securities Law but would not be subject to criminal charges unless they were used by brokers to illegally compensate the clients for stock trading losses, the lawyer said. Nomura president Junichi Ujiie admitted on Thursday at a Finance Ministry hearing that Nomura had done illegal deals for Koike. The ministry is expected to announce soon its administrative penalties against Nomura, caught in its second scandal in six years.

The scandal has led to more than a dozen arrests including former Nomura president Hideo Sakamaki and executives from Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd (DKB), one of Japan's biggest banks. Japanese media said former DKB chairman Tadashi Okuda would be indicted on Friday for allegedly arranging illegal bank loans to Koike.
